newsitem.title: CHINA: China, U.S. call talks productive, wide-ranging.
newsitem.headline: China, U.S. call talks productive, wide-ranging.

text.p: U.S. Vice President Al Gore described his talks with Chinese Premier Li Peng on Tuesday as productive and energetic and cited non-proliferation of weapons of mass destruction as a crucial U.S. goal.

China's Li, speaking after one hour of closed-door talks with Gore in the cavernous Great Hall of the People, underlined the importance of long-troubled Sino-U.S. ties but urged Washington to play a more positive role.
"We had a very productive and energetic talk," Gore told reporters after the first meetings on Tuesday.
"There are a number of issues that I would like to discuss... all of them are issues that can best be discussed here among ourselves," Gore said.

He did not say whether he raised the thorny issues of human rights and alleged Chinese donations to the Democratic presidential re-election campaign last year, but stressed the importance of maintaining a peace process.
"The non-proliferation of weapons of mass destruction is a critical goal of the United States," Gore said, but did not elaborate.
"China has high respect for the United States," Li said after his meeting with the highest-ranking official to visit China since then-president George Bush in early 1989.
But he sounded a note of caution, reflecting China's concern about superpower politics.
"We believe the United States, the biggest developed country in the world, should play a more positive role in international affairs," Li said.
"The importance of our relations serves the interestes of both peoples," he said..

"We also attach importance to Sino-U.S. relations, believing that the improvement of our relatioinship serves both peoples... Therefore I sincerely wish your visit to China complete success," Li said.

In a sign of rapidly improving ties between the world's top superpower and its fastest-growing Pacific neighbour, the two leaders witnessed the signing of two multi-million dollar contracts for U.S. business in China.
Boeing Co signed a contract to sell five 777-200 jets worth $685 million to China's international carrier, Air China.

Analysts said the Chinese decision to buy the new-generation airliners now was almost certainly based not only on aviation needs but on a thaw in ties since Sino-U.S. relations chilled in 1995 and early 1996 amid disputes over human rights and Taiwan.
In the Boeing deal, five of the 777-200s are to be delivered to Air China by the end of 1998 and the other two in 1999.
Gore and Li also witnessed signing of a formal agreement in which General Motors Corp will enter into a long-delayed joint venture with Shanghai Automotive Industry Corp to build medium-sized cars.
The $1.3 billion motor project in Shanghai will be shared equally by the two corporations. The pact won initial go-ahead in 1995 but final approval was subject to lengthy delays.

Officials dismissed reports that Gore hesitated to attend the ceremony because of allegations that China had tried to influence last year's U.S. presidential election by illegally funnelling cash to support President Bill Clinton's campaign.

Gore's meetings with Beijing leaders are aimed at strengthening a recent Sino-U.S. rapprochement, but his talks appeared likely to be darkened by the scandal over alleged Chinese funding of U.S. Democratic Party politicians.

The Washington Post has reported that the Federal Bureau of Investigation warned six members of Congress last year that they had been targeted by China to receive illegal campaign contributions from foreign corporations.
